title: Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Extension to Establish Keys for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP)
summary: Describes a DTLS extension to establish keys for SRTP and SRTCP flows. The keying happens on the media path, independent of any out-of-band signaling. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5764 explains how two endpoints use a DTLS handshake to agree on keys for protecting RTP and RTCP media. The handshake establishes the keys, while SRTP protects the media packets themselves.

questions: how are srtp keys established with dtls
how does dtls-srtp tell dtls from rtp packets
which srtp protection profiles does rfc 5764 define
subtitle: DTLS negotiates the keys; SRTP protects the real-time media packets.

tldr.problem: SRTP protects real-time media but does not establish its own keys or negotiate protection settings.
tldr.mechanism: The two endpoints run a DTLS handshake on the media path, negotiate an SRTP protection profile, and derive separate sending keys for each direction.
tldr.outcome: Media travels as SRTP packets rather than DTLS application-data records. RFC 5764 has been updated by RFC 7983 and RFC 9443.

today: RFC 5764 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7983 and RFC 9443. Read those updates with this specification.

sections.title: Why Combine DTLS and SRTP
sections.content:
Secure RTP (SRTP) can provide confidentiality, message authentication and replay protection for RTP and RTCP traffic. It does not manage keys, so another mechanism must exchange master keys and agree on algorithms and parameters.

Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) includes key management and negotiation, but its general data format is less tailored to RTP. This specification uses DTLS to establish the security settings and SRTP to protect the media.
sections.plainLanguage: SRTP protects media packets but does not arrange the keys. This RFC uses a DTLS handshake to agree on keys, then SRTP protects the media.

sections.title: Sessions and Media Directions
sections.content:
A DTLS-SRTP session connects exactly two participants and protects traffic carried over one UDP source-and-destination port pair. The peers establish a DTLS association on that pair, then use its keying material for SRTP.

A session has one SRTP context for one-way media or two contexts when media flows in both directions. The client and server use distinct keys for packets they send. RTP and RTCP can use separate port pairs, or can share a port when multiplexed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each session connects two endpoints over a particular pair of ports. Each direction has its own SRTP keys, and separate port pairs need separate DTLS-SRTP sessions.

sections.title: Choosing an SRTP Protection Profile
sections.content:
The client asks to use SRTP by including the use_srtp extension in its DTLS ClientHello. It lists acceptable protection profiles in preference order and may include a Master Key Identifier (MKI), which tells a receiver which key protected a packet.

The server selects one profile from the client's list and returns it in its own use_srtp extension. If no profile is shared, it omits the extension; the connection then uses the negotiated DTLS cipher suite unless the server rejects that result. RFC 5764 defines four profiles and limits an MKI to 255 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The client lists the SRTP protection choices it can use. The server picks one of those choices, and both endpoints use that choice for the media.

sections.title: Deriving and Replacing Media Keys
sections.content:
DTLS records and SRTP packets use different keys. A TLS exporter with the label EXTRACTOR-dtls_srtp produces separate master keys and salts for client-to-server and server-to-client traffic; SRTP derives packet-protection keys from them.

Each profile limits one key set to 2^31 packets, counting RTP and RTCP separately. At the limit, a new DTLS session should establish replacement keys and the old keys must no longer protect or validate traffic. During rekeying, receivers should retain older key sets temporarily because packets can arrive out of order.
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake supplies separate key material for each direction. When a key set reaches its packet limit, the endpoints replace it and may keep the earlier keys briefly for delayed packets.

sections.title: Sending and Sorting Packets
sections.content:
SRTP processing must wait until the DTLS handshake finishes. After negotiation, an RTP or RTCP packet is passed through DTLS to the SRTP processing, then sent as one SRTP datagram without DTLS record framing. Other DTLS control messages keep ordinary DTLS framing and use separate datagrams.

DTLS, SRTP and STUN can share a port. When these are the packet types present, the receiver distinguishes them by the first byte: values 0 or 1 indicate STUN, values 20 through 63 indicate DTLS, and values 128 through 191 indicate RTP or multiplexed RTCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the handshake finishes, media goes out as SRTP packets without a DTLS wrapper. The receiver checks the first byte to decide whether a packet belongs to STUN, DTLS or RTP.

sections.title: Security Boundaries and Multi-Party Calls
sections.content:
The DTLS handshake protects negotiation of the SRTP extension, so an attempt to force a downgrade is detected. Separate authentication keys protect DTLS and SRTP framing, reducing packet-confusion attacks to forging a valid authentication code.

DTLS-SRTP is designed for unicast, point-to-point media. A conference mixer can use a separate protected flow with each participant, but must decrypt and re-encrypt media for each recipient because each flow has its own keys. The RFC also discusses the small extra decryption cost of trying several key sets during rekeying.
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake protects the choice of SRTP settings, and separate keys protect the two packet formats. A mixer uses separate keys for each participant's flow, so it must process media between those flows.
